29.title: the inner-base store has no guard: the same TCP data-offset byte moves through a tunnel on all five measured kernels
29.claim: The transport base is guarded and the inner base is not: the TCP data-offset byte that `nft_th_write_ok()` refuses at `@th` is written at `@ih` through a tunnel, on all five measured kernels, and the store keeps the packet's verdict.
29.repro: instrument `differ551`; one rule in the `ip` forward chain on a VXLAN frame (inner base at skb offset 42, the doff byte at inner offset 54, frame byte 96): `@th,96,8` against `@ih,432,8`.
29.expected: `nft_payload_set_eval()` calls `nft_th_write_ok()` for the transport base and nothing for the inner base; `nft_payload_csum_write_ok()` returns true for the inner base, on the comment that real L3/L4 headers cannot be mangled.
29.actual: `@ih,432,8` is applied and delivered 10/10 on 7.2.15, 7.3, 7.3.4, 7.3.4+P549 and 7.3.4+P548 (doff 50 to 60 at frame byte 96); `@th,96,8` changes nothing on the four later kernels and is applied on 7.2.15.
29.limits: IPv6 inner headers, tunnel types other than VXLAN, Geneve and ipip, and GSO/CHECKSUM_PARTIAL were not measured; the rule needs root in the initial user namespace, so this is a gap in a guard, not an attack surface.
29.regression: The byte at inner transport offset 12 is refused by the transport-base guard and written by the inner-base store; a test that pins the two bases to the same verdict would catch a regression in either direction.

30.title: the network-header guard is an offset whitelist: `ip6 ecn set` and `ip6 flowlabel set` are silently dead while their IPv4 twins work
30.claim: `nft_nh_write_ok()` is a whitelist of seven offsets for IPv4 and five for IPv6, so nft's own `ip6 ecn set` and `ip6 flowlabel set` spellings land off it and are refused silently, while the IPv4 twins are rounded to an accepted cell and applied.
30.repro: instrument `differ552`; 30 nft spellings (`ip dscp set`, `ip6 ecn set`, `ip6 flowlabel set`, raw `@nh` cells) one rule at a time, in the `ip`/`ip6` forward chain, counter and NFLOG after the store.
30.expected: `ll` is a boundary (`offset_end <= skb_network_offset`), `nh` is a switch on `priv->offset` over {0,1,4,8,10,12,16}; `stmt_evaluate_payload_need_csum()` rounds every IPv4 network store to an even width at an even offset because `proto_ip` carries `checksum_key`, and `proto_ip6` does not.
30.actual: 30 spellings on 7.2.15, 7.3, 7.3.4 and two patched 7.3.4 builds: 12 dead, identical on all five kernels. `ip6 ecn set 1` is 1 byte at offset 1 and is refused (NFT_BREAK); `ip ecn set` becomes 2 bytes at offset 0 and survives. Under `policy drop`, a rule that reads "mark ECN, then accept" drops every IPv6 packet (counter 0, nothing delivered).
30.limits: Only the spellings nft 1.1.7 generates for the declared fields were measured; other off-list stores are covered by the grid in F33.
30.regression: `ip6 ecn set` and `ip6 flowlabel set` must either be accepted at the cell they name or refused with an error; a test that installs each spelling and reads the byte back pins this.

31.title: the store guard switches on the envelope, not on the write
31.claim: Which branch of `nft_nh_write_ok()` judges a store is decided by the family, the chain label and the packet's ethertype, not by the write; at the netdev ingress hook the guard is a constant, at the bridge hook the same bytes are refused under an IPv4 label and accepted under an ARP label.
31.repro: instrument `differ553`; one rule at a time at the netdev ingress hook and at the bridge prerouting hook, one forwarded IPv4 datagram or one ARP-labelled frame; counter read from the rule itself, frame bytes from an NFLOG tap.
31.expected: `nft_nh_write_ok()` returns true before the `pf` switch when `pkt->hook == NF_INET_INGRESS`; the netdev family has an ingress hook (constant) and an egress hook (a switch on `skb->protocol`); the bridge branch switches on the chain label's ethertype.
31.actual: At ingress `@nh,336,16 set 0xCAFE` (network offset 42) has counter 1 and frame bytes 56-57 = ca fe; `ip length set 0x0030` has counter 1 at ingress and counter 0 in the `ip` family; `@nh,64,32` has counter 2 with no byte changed. At the bridge hook, the same 4-byte store at offset 8 is applied under the ARP label (bytes 22, 24, 25 changed on the IPv4 header), refused under the IPv4 and 0x9100 labels, and `ip daddr set` is dead under the ARP label.
31.limits: IPv6 inside these envelopes, the `arp` family itself, PPPoE/QinQ stacks; the netdev egress hook is measured in F33, not here.
31.regression: Every door applies the same verdict to the same `(offset,len)` store on the same bytes; the cell table in F33 is the reference a test should pin.

32.title: the arp family: four declared fields are silently dead, and the output hook adds a 28-byte bound
32.claim: The ARP branch takes only `(offset,len)`: four of nft's nine declared ARP fields are silently dead, and at the output hook the branch additionally bounds the store by the 28-byte ARP message.
32.repro: instrument `differ555`; nine declared `arp` fields and a 96-cell `(offset,len)` grid at the input hook plus 12 cells at the output hook, one rule at a time, counter and NFLOG after the store.
32.expected: `nft_nh_write_ok_arp()` receives only `const struct nft_payload_set *priv` and its predicate is `(off == 6 && len == 2) || (off >= 8 && len <= 20)`; offsets 0, 2, 4 and 5 are neither the `ar_op` case nor `>= sizeof(struct arphdr)`.
32.actual: Four declared fields are dead (`htype`, `ptype`, `hlen`, `plen`: counter 0, no log); five are applied (`operation` byte 7 01->02, `saddr ether` byte 13 66->99, `saddr ip` byte 17 09->42, `daddr ether` six bytes, `daddr ip` byte 25 01->09). The predicate reproduced over 96 input-hook cells and 12 output-hook cells.
32.limits: IPv6 over ARP envelopes and the bridge/netdev dispatchers are measured in F33; the rule needs root in the initial user namespace.
32.regression: The guard's accept-set is exactly `(6,2)` plus `off>=8 && len<=20` at the input hook, and four declared fields never reach a byte.

33.title: one guard, four types: what each branch of `nft_nh_write_ok()` actually is
33.claim: Measured on one 40-cell grid in one boot, the four branches of `nft_nh_write_ok()` are: two finite whitelists of points with per-point bounds (`ip4` 14/40, `ip6` 12/40), a point plus a half-plane (`arp` 25/40), and two dispatchers that hand the decision to one of them (`bridge`, `netdev` egress, `default` refuse); at ingress the guard is a constant true.
33.repro: instrument `differ556`, modes `f556bare`, `f556e`, `f556nd`; the same 40-cell `(offset,len)` grid through eleven envelopes in one boot, the kernel's own counter placed after the store as the oracle per cell.
33.expected: Each branch's source: `ip4` seven `case`s, `ip6` five `case`s, `arp` a point plus a half-plane, `bridge`/`netdev` switches on label or `skb->protocol` with `default: return false`, and `nft_in_ingress()` returning true before the switch.
33.actual: `ip4` 14/40, `ip6` 12/40, `nd` 40/40 (ingress constant), `eg4` 14/40, `egA` 25/40, `br4` 14/40, `brA` 25/40, `arp` 25/40; the identities `ip4 = br4 = eg4`, `arp = brA = egA` hold cell by cell. In the netdev family the egress hook is live and its column equals the ip4/arp column.
33.limits: Not measured: the `@th` and `@ll` guards on the same grid, and any family outside the five columns.
33.regression: Each envelope's accept-set is a fixed subset of the 40-cell grid; a change in any branch moves exactly one column.
33.final_note: F31's netdev branch is not dead code: the netdev family has an egress hook, where the branch is live (this section's eg4/egA columns).

35.title: the `@ll` boundary is the envelope's link-header length, and it is 0 inside an L3 tunnel
35.claim: `nft_ll_write_ok()` is `off + len <= skb_network_header - skb_mac_header + vlan_hlen`, so the bound is the current envelope's link-header length: 14 on bare Ethernet, 18 with a tag, and 0 inside an L3 tunnel where the write can only end at offset 0.
35.repro: instrument `differ557`, fifteen modes; a `(offset,len)` grid through seven envelopes in one boot, bytes read back through NFLOG, verdicts from the kernel counters.
35.expected: The guard substitutes to `priv->offset + priv->len <= skb_network_header - skb_mac_header + vlan_hlen`, i.e. the write must end inside the envelope's link header.
35.actual: The boundary measured on bare Ethernet is 14 (14 accepted, 16 refused); with a tag in metadata it is 18; inside an ipip tunnel `skb_network_offset()` is 0 and every store with a non-zero end is refused.
35.limits: Devices whose link header is not 14 bytes, and the `@nh` guard on the same grid.
35.regression: The link-layer guard is a boundary at the envelope's own link-header length; a test pins the accepted/refused cells per envelope.

36.title: in the ip family the tag is gone from the frame by the hook, in every envelope
36.claim: At the `ip`/`ip6` hooks the 802.1Q tag is in `skb` metadata, not in the frame bytes, so the link-layer store lands at `skb->data + priv->offset - 18`; a rule can rewrite the ethertype of a forwarded frame, and a store the guard cannot see is refused.
36.repro: instrument `differ558`, modes `f558bytes`, `f558ipv6`, `f558vlan`, `f558why`; a bridge at `br0` forwarding a tagged frame, one store per arm at the bridge prerouting hook, bytes read at both ports.
36.expected: `nft_payload_set_eval()` treats a frame whose tag sits in metadata specially: for `offset >= offsetof(struct vlan_ethhdr, h_vlan_encapsulated_proto)` it returns true with `vlan_hlen = VLAN_HLEN` and falls through to the ordinary store.
36.actual: Store (16,2)=0x0806 has counter 1 and the forwarded frame leaves with ethertype 0x0806 instead of 0x0800; (14,2)=0x0000 has counter 1, changes no frame byte and clears `skb->vlan_tci`, so the next hop sees the frame untagged; (12,4)=0x8100 0x0000 has counter 1 with the same effect through `__vlan_hwaccel_put_tag()`; the same (16,2) on an untagged frame is refused, counter 0.
36.limits: Only the `ip` family and a bridge forwarding path; ARP under the same envelope is F31's table.
36.regression: A tagged forwarded frame's ethertype and tag state after a `@ll` store are the same on the wire and in the skb; a test compares the egress frame with the rule's named field.

37.title: one device bit decides whether the 802.1Q tag exists in the frame at all
37.claim: For a frame whose tag the receive path pulled into metadata, `@ll` offsets are wire offsets and the four bytes the guard opens up are the tag; a two-byte store at (12,2) can leave a frame with no ethertype while the kernel still treats it as IPv4.
37.repro: instrument `differ559`, eight modes; bridge prerouting, one veth pair, one frame per arm, frames read on the egress wire.
37.expected: `nft_payload_set_eval()` subtracts `vlan_hlen` from the skb offset and `nft_ll_write_ok()` adds it back; `nft_payload_set_vlan()` handles `h_vlan_proto` for len 2; `vlan_hw_offload_capable()` knows only 0x8100 and 0x8021ad.
37.actual: Control 8100 0064 0800; `@ll,16,2=0806` gives 8100 0064 0806 (tag untouched); `@ll,14,2=0099` writes the TCI; `@ll,12,4=81000000` writes 8100 0000 0800; `@ll,16,2` on an untagged frame is refused (16+2 > 14), counter 0. `@ll,12,2 = 0` leaves the wire with ethertype 0x0000 while `skb->protocol` stays 0x0800 and the bridge keeps forwarding.
37.limits: The untagged and single-tag cases only; Q-in-Q is F39, and the `@ll` read side is F52-F56.
37.regression: Tagged and untagged frames carrying the same L2 bytes must receive the same verdict at the same cells.

38.title: the receive side of the tag: the guard judges `skb->vlan_all`, and sixteen ethertype bits pick the boundary
38.claim: The 802.1Q tag is popped before every hook, so the link-layer guard judges `skb->vlan_all` and `skb->protocol`; two frames with the same L2 bytes get different verdicts on two cells from the two ethertype bytes alone.
38.repro: instrument `differ560`, five modes; one frame at a time through bridge prerouting, bridge input, ip6 prerouting and netdev ingress, verdicts from counters, bytes from taps and NFLOG.
38.expected: `__netif_receive_skb_core()` runs `eth_type_vlan()` and `skb_vlan_untag()` before the taps and before `nf_ingress`; `eth_type_vlan()` knows ETH_P_8021Q and ETH_P_8021AD only.
38.actual: A tagged frame reaches the far side byte-identical to the untagged one (60 bytes on both taps) while the wire differs by four bytes; a 9100 frame is not popped and arrives at 64 bytes. The plain and 9100 frames give the same 36-cell set (23/36); the tagged and vid-0 frames give 25/36.
38.limits: Other TPIDs and the `@nh` base on the same frames.
38.regression: The tag's presence in the frame is decided before the hook; the guard's cells follow `skb_vlan_tag_present()`.

39.title: 802.1AD and Q-in-Q: a second TPID changes no link-layer cell, and the bridge guard refuses a two-tag frame 0/40
39.claim: A 802.1Q frame and a 802.1AD frame are indistinguishable to every branch of the guard; a Q-in-Q frame is refused by all 40 network-base cells because one `skb_vlan_untag()` leaves `skb->protocol == 0x8100`, for which the bridge branch has no case.
39.repro: instrument `differ561`, six modes; a bridge with two veth pairs, the 36-cell packet-relative grid and the 40-cell network-base grid per envelope, plus a `meta protocol` expression in front of the store.
39.expected: `nft_nh_write_ok_bridge()` switches on the label; there is no case for 0x8100, so `default: return false`. `nft_meta_pktinfo_may_update()` reads `h_vlan_encapsulated_proto` at `mac_header + 16`, which after one pop is the real ethertype.
39.actual: 802.1Q and 802.1AD give the same 25 cells of the 36-cell grid and the same 14 of the 40-cell grid; Q-in-Q is refused 0/40 while `meta protocol` reports 0x0800; with `meta protocol` before the store the same grid goes from 0 to 12 live cells, each landing four bytes before the field it names.
39.limits: 802.1ad egress and the `@ll` base; a rule needs root in the initial user namespace.
39.regression: A two-tag frame is judged in the same coordinates as a one-tag frame, or is refused with a case that names it.

40.title: the read side of `@nh`: the repair moves the read and leaves the store
40.claim: After `meta protocol` on a Q-in-Q frame, the `@nh` read and the `@nh` store use different reference points: the read lands at `data + nhoff + off`, the store at `skb_network_offset + off`, four bytes apart, so a cell compares one field and writes another.
40.repro: instrument `differ562`, six modes; 657 arms in each of two boots at bridge prerouting, a 40-cell read+compare grid and the store grid on the same Q-in-Q frame.
40.expected: `nft_payload_eval()` computes `skb_network_offset(skb) + pkt->nhoff`; `nft_payload_set_eval()` uses `skb_network_offset(skb)`; `nft_nh_write_ok_ip4()` also uses `priv->offset + skb_network_offset()`.
40.actual: The read grid is 40/40 live in every envelope and lands at `data + nhoff + off`; the store is not repaired: cell (8,1) compares the ttl and writes the IP id, cell (16,4) compares the daddr and writes the saddr. A rule that stores and then reads the same cell is dead on a plain frame and live on Q-in-Q.
40.limits: Only the Q-in-Q and PPPoE carriers of `nhoff` were measured; the `@ll` and `@th` bases are F43-F53.
40.regression: For every `@nh` cell the byte read and the byte written are the same byte; a test reads back the cell the rule names.

41.title: `meta protocol` moves the `@nh` read and not the store, and the ARP frame the guard approves dies
41.claim: On PPPoE, `meta protocol` sets `nhoff = PPPOE_SES_HLEN`, so the `@nh` read lands on the real IPv4 header and the store lands eight bytes earlier; the store grid is the IPv4 whitelist, 14/40, and not one of the 14 cells writes the field it names.
41.repro: instrument `differ563`, seven modes; 438 arms in each of two boots at bridge prerouting on a real PPPoE session frame (`8864 | ver/type code | sid | length | 0x0021 | IPv4/UDP`), plus a real PPP unit on the receiving side.
41.expected: `nft_meta_pktinfo_may_update()` sets `nhoff = PPPOE_SES_HLEN` (8) for ETH_P_PPP_SES; the read adds `pkt->nhoff`, the store does not; the whitelist is written in the coordinates of the field name.
41.actual: The read grid is 40/40 live at `data + nhoff + off` and 40/40 dead at the store's coordinate; with `meta protocol` the store grid is 14/40 and every accepted cell writes a PPPoE or preceding IPv4 field instead of the named one, e.g. (0,2) writes the PPPoE version/type at offset 14, (8,1) writes the IP version/ihl at offset 22.
41.limits: IPv6 over PPPoE and the egress doors; a rule needs root in the initial user namespace.
41.regression: On a PPPoE frame the byte a `@nh` cell names is the byte the store writes, or the store is refused.

42.title: a bridge `@nh` write reaches a real IP stack through PPPoE in the PPPOX_BOUND state
42.claim: On a real PPPoE session delivered to a real PPP unit in PPPOX_BOUND, a bridge `@nh` store lands eight bytes before the field it names and is seen by the IP stack: an `ip id` store becomes the PPPoE length and the frame dies in `ip_rcv`, and in the IPv6 branch one cell rewrites the PPP protocol.
42.repro: instrument `differ564`, modes `f564b`, `f564l`, `f564v`; one rule at a time, one PPPoE session frame at a time, a real `/dev/ppp` unit built with PPPIOCNEWUNIT/PPPIOCATTCHAN/PPPIOCCONNECT and moved to PPPOX_BOUND, a real UDP socket and the kernel counters.
42.expected: `nft_meta_pktinfo_may_update()` gives `nhoff = PPPOE_SES_HLEN + skb_network_offset`; the read uses it and the store does not, so the store is eight bytes early; the whitelist cells are the IPv4 field coordinates.
42.actual: Payload 10.1.0.1 -> 10.9.0.7:5000, 18 bytes of 0x77: `ip id = 0x0004` makes the PPPoE length 4, ppp0 hands the IP stack 2 bytes and `ip_rcv` counts InHdrErrors 1; `ip id = 0x9091` makes `skb->len < length` and `pppoe_rcv` drops the frame before the socket; (0,2) and (1,1) write the PPPoE version/code bytes and the datagram is delivered intact.
42.limits: One PPPoE session layout, IPv4 and IPv6 payloads only; not a vulnerability, because the rule needs root in the initial user namespace.
42.regression: A `@nh` store on a PPPoE frame either reaches the field it names or is refused; no cell may write the PPPoE header under an IP field name.

43.title: `@th` is refused or exact: read and store share `nft_thoff(pkt)`
43.claim: The transport base has no half-way state: read and store take the same `nft_thoff(pkt)` coordinate, so a cell either lands exactly on the field it names or is refused because `pktinfo` was never built.
43.repro: instrument `differ565`, modes `f565c`, `f565g`, `f565t`, `f565v`; 126 arms × 2 boots, four envelopes (bare, 802.1Q, Q-in-Q, PPPoE) carrying the same IPv4/UDP datagram, one rule at a time at bridge prerouting.
43.expected: `nft_payload_eval()` and `nft_payload_set_eval()` both use `offset = nft_thoff(pkt)`; `pkt->thoff = skb_network_offset + nhoff + iph->ihl*4`, and the only question is whether `NFT_PKTINFO_L4PROTO` was built.
43.actual: 8 cells per block: bare Ethernet 8/8 live, 802.1Q 8/8, Q-in-Q 0/8 without `meta protocol` and 8/8 with it (sport at frame bytes 38..39), PPPoE 0/8 without and 8/8 with it (bytes 42..43). The store lands exactly on the named field in every live cell.
43.limits: `@th` in the inet and netdev families, where `thoff` is built by other constructors (F44/F45).
43.regression: Read and store share one transport coordinate; a test pins the byte offset per envelope.

44.title: four pktinfo constructors, one coordinate
44.claim: The four `pktinfo` constructors produce one coordinate: whether `thoff` is computed relative to `skb->data` or absolute, it lands on the same wire byte at every door, because `skb->data` is the network header at these hooks.
44.repro: instrument `differ566`, modes `diag`, `dp`, `gd`, `md`, `rf`, `td`, `tm`; 348 arms × 2 boots, four doors (ip L3, inet L3, netdev ingress, inet ingress) with two base chains per door, `@th` read and store per cell.
44.expected: `nft_set_pktinfo_ipv4()` gives `thoff = ip_hdrlen(skb)`; `__nft_set_pktinfo_ipv4_validate()` gives `skb_network_offset + nhoff + ihl*4`; the ingress constructor gives `ihl*4`; the bridge one uses the validate constructor. `skb->data` is the network header at these hooks.
44.actual: Eight `@th` cells per door and envelope: the store is accepted and the byte read back is the same on all four doors; the two constructors' coordinates coincide on every cell.
44.regression: All pktinfo constructors agree on the transport offset for the same frame; a test compares the byte written through each door.

45.title: IPv6 does not compute `@th`, it walks for it
45.claim: IPv6 builds the transport coordinate by walking extension headers (`ipv6_find_hdr()`), not by a formula; the coordinate is right when the walk succeeds, and the walk's three failure modes carry three different verdicts at the doors.
45.repro: instrument `differ567`, ten modes; 524 arms × 2 boots, five doors (ip L3 as control, ip6 L3, inet L3, netdev ingress, inet ingress), eight `@th` cells per door and envelope, plus extension-header frames.
45.expected: `nft_set_pktinfo_ipv6()` walks with `ipv6_find_hdr(..., IP6_FH_F_AUTH)`; the validate constructor walks after a version and payload-length check; the ingress constructor returns -1 on failure, which becomes NF_DROP.
45.actual: The coordinate follows the walk and equals the `skb_copy_bits()` offset wanted; the three failures (a bad version, a truncated header, an unknown next header) are refused at the validate doors and dropped at the ingress door.
45.limits: IPv6 fragments and the egress half; the `@nh`/`@ll` bases in IPv6 are F47-F59.
45.regression: The transport base in IPv6 equals the end of the extension-header walk; a test pins one cell per extension-header shape.

46.title: `@ll` depends on who built the skb, not on the door
46.claim: The link-layer base is resolved from `skb_mac_header()` and refused outright when the MAC header was never set, so away from the receive path the same offset is live, dead or erased according to the traffic class that built the skb.
46.repro: instrument `differ568`, seven modes; 428 arms × 2 boots, six doors (inet local_out, postrouting, forward, prerouting, input and netdev egress), three traffic classes, twelve `@ll` cells each.
46.expected: `@ll` stores are resolved as `skb_mac_header(skb) - skb->data` and refused when `skb_mac_header_was_set()` is false; the header checksum is computed before the hook.
46.actual: Twelve cells per door and class: local datagrams 0/12 at local_out, postrouting 0/12; forwarded frames 10/12 at postrouting, forward and prerouting with the store erased for one class; delivered frames 10/12 at prerouting and input. The receiving bytes and counters agree.
46.limits: Tunnels and devices without an Ethernet header (F49/F50); GSO/CHECKSUM_PARTIAL is F60/F61.
46.regression: `@ll` is accepted exactly where a MAC header exists and the write ends inside it; a test pins the cell table per traffic class.

47.title: a hop-limit store at `@nh` is free at six of seven egress door/class pairs
47.claim: The IPv6 network-base list has no case for offset 4 and none for offset 6, so a payload-length or next-header store is refused everywhere while a hop-limit store is free at six of the seven door/class pairs.
47.repro: instrument `differ569`, mode `iso`; 112 arms × 2 boots, six doors and two classes, `@nh` cells per door with the frame's bytes and the receiving socket as witnesses.
47.expected: The IPv6 branch of `nft_nh_write_ok()` is a switch with `case 0` comparing the version nibble, `case 2`, `case 8`, `case 24`; there is no case for 4 or 6.
47.actual: `@nh,4,2` (payload_len) and `@nh,6,1` (next header) are refused at every door; `@nh,7,1` (hop limit) is accepted at six of seven door/class pairs and the datagram is delivered with the stored value; `@nh,0,4` with a non-6 version nibble is refused.
47.limits: Only the cells listed in the section; TCP and tunnels were not measured.
47.regression: The IPv6 whitelist's accepted offsets are exactly {0,1,2,8,24}; a test stores at 4 and 6 and expects a refusal.

48.title: at an egress door `meta protocol` puts a PPPoE frame into two different coordinate systems
48.claim: On a PPPoE frame at the netdev egress hook, `meta protocol` computes `nhoff = 8 + skb_network_offset` (22) while the IPv6 constructor reads the version byte at `skb_network_offset + nhoff` (36, which is `saddr[6]`) and the transport walk starts at 22; the same expression therefore gives the transport base the right answer and the network base the wrong one.
48.repro: instrument `differ570`, modes `ppp6e`, `th6`; 25 arms × 2 boots on a kernel-built PPPoE frame (PF_PPPOX session socket, sid 99, IPv6/UDP payload), one rule at a time at the netdev egress hook.
48.expected: `nft_meta_pktinfo_may_update()` sets `nhoff = PPPOE_SES_HLEN + skb_network_offset`; `__nft_set_pktinfo_ipv6_validate()` reads the version byte at `skb_network_offset + nhoff` while `ipv6_find_hdr()` starts at `nhoff`; a failed version check calls `nft_set_pktinfo_unspec()`, which resets `nhoff` to 0.
48.actual: `meta protocol` reports 0x86dd and `meta l4proto` reports nothing; `@nh,7,1` and `@th,0,2` are both refused, for two different reasons (`nft_nh_write_ok_netdev()` has no ETH_P_PPP_SES case; `pkt->flags` is 0); after the failed version check, `@nh` falls back to the PPPoE header.
48.limits: One PPPoE layout and the netdev egress hook; the bridge PPPoE path is F41/F42.
48.regression: At one door `meta protocol` yields one coordinate for every base; a test reads the version byte and the hop limit through `@nh` and `@th` and compares them with the frame.

49.title: at a ppp0 layer-3 door the base is right and `@ll` does not exist
49.claim: Once the PPP layer has run, the `@ll` base does not collapse onto `@nh`: it disappears, because `skb_mac_header_len()` is 0 while the network header is present; the same `@nh` cell that is refused at one door is a single byte of the header at another.
49.repro: instrument `differ571`, modes `ctl`, `rd`, `tapf`, `wr`; one 88-byte frame (ethernet | PPPoE sid 99 | 00 57 | IPv6/UDP) seen at four doors in one boot: inet prerouting and ip6 prerouting on ppp0, netdev ingress on the veth, and an ip prerouting chain that never sees it.
49.expected: `ppp_receive_nonmp_frame()` resets `mac_header` to `skb->data` and the receive path calls `skb_reset_mac_len()`, so `skb_mac_header_len()` is 0; `nft_ll_write_ok()` then refuses every non-zero end.
49.actual: At the ppp0 layer-3 doors `skb_network_offset()` and `pkt->nhoff` are both 0: `@nh,0,4` reads 60 00 00 00, `@nh,4,2` the payload length, `@nh,7,1` the hop limit 40. At the netdev ingress door the same cells read 11 00 00 63 and 57 (the PPPoE header and PPP protocol). `@ll` is refused at ppp0 for every non-zero end.
49.limits: Only the ppp0 device and one frame layout; PPPoE at the bridge is F41/F42.
49.regression: A device with no link-layer header refuses `@ll` and keeps `@nh` correct; a test pins both.

50.title: a device without an ethernet header can never carry `@ll` into a bridge
50.claim: `@ll` has two domains at one bridge door: reads run past the link header into the network header while writes stop at `mac_len`, and the guard's verdict is the same at two doors whose consequences are opposite because by the time the layer-3 door runs, the copies for the other ports are already cloned; a ppp device cannot be put in a bridge at all (`br_add_if()` rejects `ARPHRD_ETHER`).
50.repro: instrument `differ572`; one 80-byte IPv6/UDP frame injected on a veth, a bridge `br0` with two ports, the same skb seen at four doors in one boot, four AF_PACKET taps.
50.expected: `br_add_if()` rejects `dev->type != ARPHRD_ETHER` with `-EINVAL`; `nft_ll_write_ok()` bounds writes at `mac_len` while `nft_payload_copy_vlan()` lets reads run past it.
50.actual: `br_add_if()` on a ppp device returns rc=-22 while the same call succeeds for both Ethernet ports; the read and store domains differ by the four bytes the guard adds, and the store at the layer-3 door does not reach the copies already made for the other ports.
50.limits: Q-in-Q on these doors and the `@nh`/`@th` bases; a rule needs root in the initial user namespace.
50.regression: A `@ll` store at a bridge door reaches exactly the copies the kernel makes after it; the read and write domains are the same or the difference is documented in the guard.

51.title: store visibility among copies, and the frame the bridge learns
51.claim: A payload store reaches exactly the copies of a frame that the kernel makes after it; for copies made before it the store is not lost by oversight but by copy-on-write -- `__skb_clone()` sets `cloned = 1` on the source as well, so `skb_ensure_writable()` copies the head and the earlier copies keep their bytes.
51.repro: instrument `differ573`; one 80-byte broadcast IPv6/UDP frame, a bridge `br0` with three ports, one rule at one of four doors (bridge prerouting, bridge forward, bridge input, ip6 prerouting), four AF_PACKET taps counting copies.
51.expected: `__skb_clone()` sets `cloned = 1` on the source; `skb_ensure_writable()` copies the head; `br_flood()` makes the port copies at a known point in the path.
51.actual: One frame: 1 at bridge prerouting, 2 at forward, 1 at LOCAL_IN, 1 at the ip6 door. A store at prerouting is accepted once and all three copies carry it; the same store at the forward door reaches neither the earlier local copy nor the other port's copy. The bridge learns the stored source MAC, so the next store into the same bytes becomes known unicast and is not flooded.
51.limits: Only bridge flooding and one frame; no QinQ or tunnels.
51.regression: A store reaches the copies made after it and no others; the neighbour/forwarding entry learned from the stored bytes is visible in the bridge table.

52.title: a tagged frame with a non-zero vid dies before the IPv6 door, and `@ll,12,2` is not the inner ethertype
52.claim: With the tag in metadata, `@ll` is not the frame: `nft_payload_copy_vlan()` rebuilds `struct vlan_ethhdr`, so the inner ethertype sits at `@ll,16`, not `@ll,12`; once a VLAN sub-interface exists the tag is cleared and the whole domain shifts four bytes earlier; a tagged frame with a non-zero vid and no VLAN device dies as `PACKET_OTHERHOST` before any IPv6 counter.
52.repro: instrument `differ574`; one bridge with three ports, one 80-byte tagged frame seen at five doors; the tag in metadata and on a VLAN sub-interface; counters from the bridge, the ip6 stack and `rx_otherhost_dropped`.
52.expected: `nft_payload_copy_vlan()` rebuilds `struct vlan_ethhdr` from `skb->vlan_proto`/`skb->vlan_tci`; `__netif_receive_skb_core()` sets `PACKET_OTHERHOST` when `skb_vlan_tag_get_id(skb) != 0` and `vlan_do_receive()` finds no VLAN device, and `ip6_rcv_core()` returns on that pkt_type before `IPSTATS_MIB_IN`.
52.actual: A vid-100 frame is counted by the bridge three times (brp 1, brf 2, brl 1), reaches the far end's ingress hook, and never reaches an IPv6 hook (ip6 prerouting 0, Ip6InReceives 0, Ip6InDiscards 0); the only counters that move are `rx_otherhost_dropped` on br0 and both ports. A store into the TCI changes no wire byte and turns the dropped frame into a delivered datagram.
52.limits: 802.1ad, two tags, `VLAN_FLAG_REORDER_HDR` cleared, and a VLAN device present are F53-F56.
52.regression: The inner ethertype is read at the offset the tag state implies, and a dropped vid is counted where the kernel drops it.

53.title: the one configuration where the kernel puts the tag back into the frame between `vlan_do_receive()` and the hook
53.claim: Clearing `VLAN_FLAG_REORDER_HDR` on a VLAN sub-interface is the one configuration in which the kernel puts the tag back into the frame bytes before a layer-3 hook; the `@ll` base there is the frame as it came off the wire and the write guard, `off + len <= mac_len`, moves four bytes with it.
53.repro: instrument `differ575`; one bridge with four VLAN sub-interfaces (two with the flag, two without), one 80-byte frame seen at ip6 prerouting and at netdev ingress, 44 arms per boot over two boots.
53.expected: `vlan_dev_hard_header()` and the reorder path decide whether the tag is bytes or a word; `mac_len` follows the same decision.
53.actual: Flag set (`br0.100`): at ip6 prerouting `@ll` reads 12 = 86dd, 14 = 6000, 16 = 0000, 18 = 001a, `mac_header` at frame 4, `mac_len` 14. Flag cleared (`br0.101`): 12 = 8100, 14 = 0065, 16 = 86dd, 18 = 6000, 20 = 0000, `mac_header` at 0, `mac_len` 18; the packet socket shows 80 bytes untagged against 84 tagged. NFULA_HWHEADER (14 bytes) and the frame disagree by four bytes for the same message.
53.limits: Nested VLANs and other device types were not measured; a store into the tag that reaches a wire is F54.
53.regression: A per-device flag moves the `@ll` domain and the guard by exactly four bytes; a test pins the offsets on both configurations.

54.title: the tag on the wire is composed by the egress device; no store into it survives
54.claim: The 802.1Q tag is a property of the device a frame leaves through: `vlan_dev_hard_header()` builds a fresh header from `vlan->vlan_id` (plus an egress QoS map of `skb->priority`), so a store into the tag bytes or the TCI at a layer-3 door does not survive; at the netdev ingress hook the same offset is `skb->vlan_tci` and the store re-targets the VLAN.
54.repro: instrument `differ576`, modes `warn`, `xf`; a VLAN sub-interface with `VLAN_FLAG_REORDER_HDR` cleared, one rule at a time, the egress frame and the far end's demux as witnesses; the second half reproduces the `invalid VLAN protocol` WARN with one rule `@ll,12,2 = 0806` at netdev ingress.
54.expected: `vlan_dev_hard_header()` writes `vlan->vlan_id | vlan_dev_get_egress_qos_mask(dev, skb->priority)` into four fresh bytes; `vlan_find_dev()` reaches `vlan_proto_idx()` only when the device has a VLAN above it, and `vlan_proto_idx()` is the function that warns.
54.actual: `@ll,14,2` writes a byte and the counter says the store was taken, yet the far end demuxes the device's vid and the priority bits do not travel; deleting the four tag bytes changes nothing on the wire. With a tag present and a `vlan_info` on the device, one rule produces one WARN line per frame and every such frame is dropped; a bare veth pair cannot warn at all.
54.limits: Only veth and one VLAN layout; the warning's exact call site is read from the source, not instrumented.
54.regression: The tag on the wire equals the egress device's configuration, not the bytes a rule wrote; a test compares the stored TCI with the wire and pins the WARN to the same condition.

55.title: the PCP is the part of the tag a hook can reach, and the channel is `skb->priority`
55.claim: Of the tag's four bytes, three bits are reachable from a rule -- the PCP -- and they are not reached through the tag at all: `meta priority set 5` plus an `egress-qos-map 5:3` puts TCI 0x6066 on the wire instead of 0x0066, witnessed by four independent readers.
55.repro: instrument `differ577`, mode `pcp`; table ip6 with `meta priority set 5` in the forward chain, one VLAN device with `egress-qos-map 5:3`, one 80-byte frame; witnesses: the egress door's NFULA_L2HDR, the receiving device's NFULA_VLAN, a far-end `@ll,14,2` read and the AF_PACKET auxdata.
55.expected: `vlan_dev_hard_header()` writes `vlan_id | vlan_dev_get_egress_qos_mask(dev, skb->priority)`; the map is a hash table whose bucket is `skprio & 0xF` but whose match is the full 32-bit value.
55.actual: TCI 0x6066 instead of 0x0066, the same number in all four witnesses. A priority value that shares the low nibble but differs above it does not match the map entry.
55.limits: The map needs CAP_NET_ADMIN over the device; only one map shape was measured.
55.regression: The PCP on the wire is a function of `skb->priority` and the device's egress map; a test pins the TCI for a given priority.

56.title: the tag is bytes or a word according to an offload bit, not the TPID
56.claim: Whether the four tag bytes are frame bytes or a word in the skb is decided by an offload capability bit (`NETIF_F_HW_VLAN_CTAG_TX` / `NETIF_F_HW_VLAN_STAG_TX`), not by the protocol; on a bridged path with VLAN devices as ports the tag is neither at any door.
56.repro: instrument `differ578`, modes `ad`, `br`; 30 arms per boot over two boots; clearing the device's TX VLAN feature with ETHTOOL_SFEATURES moves the same tag from the skb into the frame, witnessed by the packet socket, NFULA_VLAN and the egress L2 header.
56.actual: `x1.102` (vlan 102, proto 802.1ad, reorder cleared): wire 80 bytes, tag a word; with `NETIF_F_HW_VLAN_STAG_TX` cleared: wire 84 bytes, bytes 88a8 0066 86dd; `x1.103` with CTAG_TX cleared: wire 84 bytes as well. NFULA_TCI is absent in the byte case and the egress L2 header is 14 bytes with a tci word against 18 without.
56.limits: Two device types and one bridge layout; the `@ll` read side is F37/F52.
56.regression: The tag's representation follows the device's offload bits; a test flips the bit and pins the wire length and NFULA_TCI.

57.title: the privilege boundary: two gates, one line each
57.claim: Two different gates stand between a user and a payload store: `CAP_NET_ADMIN` in the namespace that owns the netns for the netlink call, and `ctx->net->user_ns == &init_user_ns` for the store itself; a process that owns its own user and network namespace can install a read-and-drop rule but not a store.
57.repro: instrument `differ579`, modes `priv`, `probe`; 19 traffic arms and four credential contexts (root in the initial netns, uid 1000 in the initial netns, uid 1000 in its own user+net namespace), each with the same four expressions.
57.expected: `nfnetlink.c` checks `netlink_net_capable(skb, CAP_NET_ADMIN)`; `nft_payload_set_init()` checks `ctx->net->user_ns != &init_user_ns` and returns -EPERM; `nft_payload_init()` (the read) and `nft_meta_set_init` have no such check.
57.actual: root in the initial netns: table 0, chain 0, read 0, store 0, meta 0 (all succeed). uid 1000 in the initial netns: -1 for all five. uid 1000 in its own user+netns: table 0, chain 0, read 0, store -1, meta 0; the same process installs a working `@ll,12,2 = 86dd` read+drop rule.
57.limits: The check is measured on this tree only; other nft objects were not swept.
57.regression: The two gates are independent: a read is available in a user-owned netns, a store is not; a test pins both errnos.

58.title: the three write guards answer three different questions, and none of them asks the length
58.claim: The three guards are an arithmetic boundary (`@ll`), a whitelist (`@nh`) and an exact coordinate (`@th`); none asks the packet's length, so outside the ingress constant the accepted set is a property of the coordinates, and the packet's own length is the only bound left at netdev ingress.
58.repro: instrument `differ580`, mode `bounds`; 55 arms × 2 boots, two hooks (netdev ingress on a veth, ip6 prerouting), one rule per arm, frame bytes read back through NFLOG.
58.expected: `nft_ll_write_ok()` is `offset <= skb_network_offset(pkt->skb)` and returns true at ingress; at a layer-3 door `skb_network_offset()` is 0, so with `offset = -mac_len + priv->offset` the check is exactly `off + len <= mac_len`.
58.actual: At ip6 prerouting on a plain Ethernet device, of nine (off,len) cells with len 2 at offsets 12..50 exactly one is accepted (12,2) and eight are refused. At netdev ingress every cell is accepted, and the frame's own length is the only bound: `@ll,18,2` writes frame bytes 14..15 (the version nibble) and produces Ip6InHdrErrors; `@ll,24,4` writes the next header, hop limit and source bytes and produces Ip6InUnknownProtos.
58.limits: Only IPv6 Ethernet frames and two hooks; the length question is answered by the cells, not by a length check in the guard.
58.regression: The accepted cells of each guard are exactly the ones its coordinate arithmetic allows; a test pins the cell tables at both hooks.

59.title: two chains on one ingress hook point get two different guards
59.claim: Two base chains on the same ingress hook point get two different guards: `nft_do_chain_inet_ingress()` rewrites `state->pf` from NFPROTO_NETDEV to the packet's family before the chain runs, so a netdev chain has unbounded `@ll`/`@nh` while an inet chain at the same point is bounded.
59.repro: instrument `differ581`, mode `guard`; 63 arms × 2 boots over six hooks (netdev ingress, inet ingress on the same device and hook point, ipv4/ipv6/inet prerouting, arp at NF_ARP_IN), one rule per arm, bytes read through NFLOG.
59.expected: `nft_ll_write_ok()` and `nft_nh_write_ok()` both test `pkt->state->pf`/`pkt->state->hook`, and `nft_do_chain_inet_ingress()` rewrites `state->pf` from NFPROTO_NETDEV to the packet's family before the chain runs.
59.actual: Same device, same frame, same hook point: `@ll,14,2` in a netdev chain writes frame byte 14 and produces Ip6InHdrErrors 1, Ip6InReceives 0, no delivery; in an inet chain it is refused (counter 1, no log message) and the frame is delivered. `@ll,16,2` and `@nh,6,1` behave the same way.
59.limits: ARP is measured only at NF_ARP_IN; other hook points were not swept.
59.regression: At one hook point the two chains' guards differ in exactly the way the `pf` rewrite requires; a test pins both verdicts.

60.title: on a CHECKSUM_PARTIAL datagram the UDP checksum field is the pseudo-header seed, and a transport-base store pays nothing
60.claim: On a datagram whose L4 checksum the stack has left for the device, the checksum field holds the pseudo-header seed (fad2 for IPv6/UDP, 14ad for IPv4/UDP) rather than the real checksum (7a78, 609e); a transport-base store on such a packet pays nothing, because the fixup block is skipped by the same clause that makes the receiver skip verification.
60.repro: instrument `differ582`, modes `opt`, `part`; 54 arms × 2 boots, one topology with two provenances of the same 18 bytes (a real UDP socket = CHECKSUM_PARTIAL, AF_PACKET = CHECKSUM_NONE), witnesses: the tap's `tp_status` (9 against 1), the rule's NFLOG bytes and a layer-3 witness chain.
60.expected: `udp6_hwcsum_outgoing()` and `udp4_hwcsum()` write `uh->check = ~csum_ipv6_magic(...)` with a zero payload contribution; the whole fixup block is guarded by `(csum_type == INET || csum_flags) && ...`.
60.actual: Checksum field fad2 (IPv6) and 14ad (IPv4) against real checksums 7a78 and 609e; `tp_status` 9 on all CHECKSUM_PARTIAL arms and 1 on the AF_PACKET twins; a transport-base store changes no byte the fixup would have touched and the datagram is delivered.
60.limits: Not measured: a real device that computes the checksum; only veth with feature bits cleared.
60.regression: The checksum field's meaning follows `ip_summed`; a test pins the field's value for both provenances.

61.title: the forwarded path with CHECKSUM_PARTIAL: who computes the checksum
61.claim: On a forwarded datagram the price of a payload write is paid by the exit device, in whatever the checksum field holds at the time, and only for packets that arrive with CHECKSUM_PARTIAL: an exit with `NETIF_F_HW_CSUM` carries the pseudo-header seed to the wire, one without it carries a true checksum.
61.repro: instrument `differ583`, mode `fwd`; 25 arms × 2 boots, ip6 forward chain of a router netns, two exit devices that differ in `NETIF_F_HW_CSUM` (bit 3, cleared with ETHTOOL_SFEATURES), two provenances of the same 80 bytes.
61.expected: `skb_checksum_help()` computes the checksum and sets `ip_summed = CHECKSUM_NONE` when the device cannot checksum; the rule's `csum type inet` fixup runs only if it is reached before that.
61.actual: With no rule: P = fad4 (to fd03::92) and fad5 (to fd04::92); the true checksums are 7a76 and 7a75. The exit with `NETIF_F_HW_CSUM` puts fad4/fad5 on the wire; the exit without it puts the true checksum. A store into the checksum field turns the receiver's verification on.
61.limits: GSO (clearing NETIF_F_HW_CSUM also clears NETIF_F_GSO_UDP_L4) is F62.
61.regression: On the forwarded path the checksum on the wire is a function of the exit device's features and the arriving `ip_summed`; a test pins both exits.

62.title: a UDP-GSO datagram with two exit devices: who segments, and who pays for a FORWARD store
62.claim: On the GSO path the price of a payload write is paid by whoever segments: an exit that keeps `NETIF_F_GSO_UDP_L4` puts one 1262-byte frame with the whole-datagram seed on the wire and the receiver cuts it, while an exit without it cuts on the way out and computes each segment's checksum from the bytes as they stand; the same store is free on one door and paid on the other.
62.repro: instrument `differ584`, mode `gso`; 25 arms × 2 boots, ip6 forward chain of a router netns, one 1200-byte UDP datagram sent with UDP_SEGMENT 512 (segments 512/512/176), two exits differing in NETIF_F_GSO_UDP_L4 and NETIF_F_HW_CSUM.
62.expected: `validate_xmit_skb()` segments only when the device lacks the feature; `__udp_gso_segment()` computes each segment's checksum from the bytes.
62.actual: With no rule, y1 puts one 1262-byte frame with checksum ff72 (fold16 of the pseudo header with length 1208) and the receiver gets 512/512/176; y2 puts three frames 574/574/238 with uh->len 520/520/184 and checksums 82af/82af/1f91 valid per frame. `@th,8,4 = a0a1a2a3` is free on y1 and paid on y2; a store into either header field the segmenter reads breaks every segment at once.
62.limits: Only veth with feature bits cleared; no real NIC.
62.regression: The number of frames on the wire and the checksum each carries are a function of the exit device's features; a test pins both exits.

63.title: GRO hands the rule a packet the sender never sent
63.claim: With Generic Receive Offload the skb a rule evaluates is one packet built out of several datagrams: its UDP header is not any datagram's header, and which header a rule reads depends on a device bit -- 0x00c3 on a router with `rx-udp-gro-forwarding`, 0xfcc2 on a router with `rx-gro-list`, for the same three datagrams and the same rule.
63.repro: instrument `differ585`, mode `aggr`; 26 arms × 2 boots, three netns (sender, router, receiver), one rule on the forward chain, two routers whose GRO doors differ in one device bit.
63.expected: `udp6_gro_complete()` completes a linear aggregate with `uh->len = total` and `uh->check = ~udp_v6_check(total, saddr, daddr, 0)`; the fraglist branch only calls `udp_set_len(uh, skb->len - nhoff)` and keeps the first datagram's checksum field.
63.actual: Same three datagrams, same rule, same table: the checksum field the rule reads is 0x00c3 through `rx-udp-gro-forwarding` and 0xfcc2 through `rx-gro-list`; a rule that matches or rewrites `@th,6,2` behaves differently on two routers that agree on everything a rule can name. A store made on an aggregate is not paid for by the fraglist splitter (`__udp_gso_segment_list()` calls `skb_segment_list()`, which copies no payload and computes no checksum).
63.limits: Only UDP over IPv6 and the two GRO doors; TCP GRO, tunnels and a real NIC were not measured.
63.regression: A rule reading the UDP header of an aggregate reads the aggregate's header, which is a function of the GRO door; a test pins both doors' values.

64.title: an aggregate presents a rule with a header that describes no datagram
64.claim: An aggregate's `uh->len` is the sum of the datagrams in it -- a length no datagram has -- and its checksum field is the first datagram's own CHECKSUM_PARTIAL seed on the fraglist path or a seed over the whole aggregate on the linear path.
64.repro: instrument `differ586`, mode `geom`; four compositions (512×3; 512×3+200; 64×512) through both GRO doors, one rule on the forward chain, the header fields read through the rule's NFLOG message.
64.expected: `udp_gro_complete()` writes `skb->len - nhoff` into `uh->len`; `skb_gro_receive()` completes the header on the linear path, `udp_gro_receive()` merges without touching the head's field on the fraglist path.
64.actual: 512,512,512 fraglist: `uh->len` 0x0608, `uh->check` fcc2 (seed of 520). 512,512,512,200 fraglist: 0x06d0, fcc2; linear: 0x06d0, 018b (seed of 1744). 64×512 fraglist: 0x8008, fcc2; linear: 0x8008, 7ac3 (seed of 32776). A rule that reads `@th,4,2` sees a length no datagram has; `@th,6,2` addresses 520 bytes of a 1744-byte packet.
64.limits: Only UDP and the two GRO doors; the trailing segment's length is F65's subject.
64.regression: For a given composition and door, `uh->len` and `uh->check` are fixed; a test pins the four combinations.

65.title: the packet that nothing follows
65.claim: A UDP datagram that begins a GRO flow and is not followed by another is not delivered when it is sent: with `gro_flush_timeout` at 200 ms it reaches the forward chain 201 ms later, and a datagram that starts a flow inside the timer's own poll reaches it one flush period later (402 ms).
65.repro: instrument `differ587`, modes `cap`, `flow`; three netns with `gro_flush_timeout` set on the ingress device, one rule that counts and logs, timestamps from the rule's own log records; 64-datagram arms for the byte cap.
65.expected: GRO holds a flow until the timer (`gro_flush_timeout`) or the poll ends the aggregation; `udp_set_len()` has a zero-length branch at GRO_LEGACY_MAX_SIZE.
65.actual: One send arrives as two packets: an aggregate whose `uh->len` is the sum of three datagrams (0x04d0) with the first datagram's seed 0xfcc2, and a plain packet with the sender's untouched header (0x0208, 0xfcc2); the second flow arrives at 402 ms. The byte cap is 65536 and counts one byte more than the payload: on the fraglist path 64 datagrams merge up to payload 1022 and at 1023 the 64th is refused (63+1); at payload 1200 the aggregate is 54+10. The largest UDP length a rule can read here is 0xff88 (65416).
65.limits: One flush timeout (200 ms) and one device; TCP GRO and a real NIC were not measured.
65.regression: Delivery time of an un-followed datagram is the flush timeout; a test pins 201 ms and the 402 ms second flow.

66.title: two ceilings, one budget
66.claim: The two merge paths test different lengths against the same 65536: the linear path counts `H + k*P` and the fraglist path `2H + k*P`, with H = 48, so with 64 datagrams the linear path merges up to payload 1023 and the fraglist up to 1022; a third 65536 that a rule cannot see is `gso_max_size`, which decides whether the aggregate leaves as one frame.
66.repro: instrument `differ588`, modes `cap`, `split`; one send of 64 equal datagrams through both doors, tails on 63 equal datagrams, and a sweep of `uh->len` at the 65536 boundary.
66.expected: `skb_gro_receive()` tests `p->len + skb_gro_len()` (payload), `skb_gro_receive_list()` tests `p->len + skb->len` before its `skb_pull()` (L3 + payload), and `p->len` grows by the payload in both.
66.actual: 64 datagrams of 1023 bytes: linear one packet (`uh->len` 0xffc8 = 65480), fraglist two (0xfbc9 and 0x0407, the second 200 ms later). Tails on 63 equal datagrams: fraglist merges up to 990 and refuses at 991; linear up to 975 and refuses at 976. `gso_features_check()`: `uh->len` 65481 (frame 65535) leaves as one frame, 65482 (65536) as sixty-four segments of 1024.
66.limits: IPv6 only for this table (IPv4 is F68); TCP GRO and a real NIC were not measured.
66.regression: For each door the last merging payload is fixed by the two inequalities; a test pins 1022/1023 and the two tails.

67.title: the head of an aggregate pays for the whole aggregate, and above half a buffer that number collapses
67.claim: Below half a receive buffer the first segment of a fraglist aggregate is charged the sum of the packets that went into it (`p->truesize += skb->truesize`), so k datagrams cost (2k-1)*s; above half a buffer `skb_condense()` overwrites the head's truesize with one datagram's price, and the refusal is decided on that smaller number.
67.repro: instrument `differ589`, modes `cond`, `dflt`; 1200-byte datagrams on five buffers, a 64-datagram arm, and a pair of buffers that differ only in whether the queue is above half; receiver reads `/proc/net/udp6` before a single recv.
67.expected: The default `rmem_max` is 212992 = (256+576)*256; `skb_gro_receive_list()` adds each arriving skb's truesize to the head; `skb_condense()` is called only when `rmem > rcvbuf >> 1` and rewrites the head's truesize to `SKB_TRUESIZE(skb_end_offset())`.
67.actual: 212992 = (256+576)*256 with 576 the only value in [512,640] that fits the two measured truesizes (1280-704, 2304-1728); `SO_RCVBUF(106496)` reproduces the default. 1200-byte datagrams: 133120 keeps 4, 143360 9, 153600 13, 163840 18, 184320 27, with 131328/142848/152064/163584/184320 bytes queued exactly; at 184320 the 27th leaves rmem equal to rcvbuf and is accepted (the test is `>`). Above half: 311296 keeps 54 of 54, 344064 keeps 25 of 54.
67.limits: Only UDP over IPv6 and one topology; TCP GRO and a real NIC were not measured.
67.regression: `rmem` after an aggregate equals the sum of the segments' prices below half a buffer and the collapsed head's price above it; a test pins both regimes.

68.title: the IPv4 twin of the GRO byte cap and of the receive-queue budget
68.claim: On IPv4 the fraglist ceiling moves by exactly 2*(48-28) = 40 bytes relative to IPv6 and the receive-queue accounting moves by nothing: 64 datagrams of 1023 bytes arrive as one packet through the fraglist door where IPv6 gives two, and the queue keeps the same numbers as IPv6 to the byte.
68.repro: instrument `differ590`, modes `cap4`, `cond4`; 25 cap arms and 10 queue arms, two attempts per arm, two boots, three netns on IPv4, a rule on the `ip` forward chain that only counts and logs, receiver reads `/proc/net/udp`.
68.expected: `skb_gro_receive()` tests `p->len + skb_gro_len()` (payload), `skb_gro_receive_list()` tests `p->len + skb->len` (L3+payload), and `p->len` grows by the payload in both: linear `H + N*P < 65536`, fraglist `2H + N*P < 65536`, H = 28 on IPv4.
68.actual: 64×1023 through the fraglist door: one packet, `uh->len` 0xffc8 = 65480, one 65514-byte frame on the wire; the same send on IPv6 gave two (0xfbc9 + 0x0407). 64×1024 splits on both families; 64×1022 merges on both. Tails on 63×1024: 995 merges (28+64512+995 = 65535), 996 splits. Queue: 212992 keeps 39 of 54 1200-byte datagrams with 211968 bytes; 133120→4, 143360→9, 153600→13, 163840→18, 184320→27; 311296/344064 keep 54 vs 25.
68.limits: IPv4 only for this table; the fraglist byte cap on IPv4 with equal-length datagrams is F69's cell.
68.regression: The 40-byte family shift is visible in exactly the one cell the arithmetic requires; the queue numbers are family-independent.

69.title: where an aggregate's price comes from, and how the byte cap actually binds
69.claim: The byte cap is reachable only when every datagram has the same length, because a length change ends the flow after one datagram; with equal lengths the fraglist cap splits 40 datagrams of 1637 bytes into 39+1 while the linear door merges them into one, and an aggregate of k datagrams is charged (2k-1)*s because the segmenter keeps the whole truesize on the head.
69.repro: instrument `differ591`, modes `cap`, `price`; 14 cap arms and 19 price arms, two attempts each, two boots; IPv4 three netns, taps on both egress doors, receiver reads `/proc/net/udp`.
69.expected: `udp_gro_receive_segment()` ends a flow when `ulen != udp_get_len_short(uh2)`; the two doors test `2H + (n+1)*P <= 65535` (fraglist) and `H + (n+1)*P <= 65535` (linear); `skb_segment_list()` subtracts len and data_len from the head and never touches truesize.
69.limits: TCP GRO, CHECKSUM_COMPLETE, tunnels and a real NIC were not measured; why one older measurement of the same aggregate came out one 1280-byte unit short is not established.
69.regression: The fraglist cap is `2H + (n+1)*P <= 65535` and the price total is `(2k-1)*s`; a test pins 39+1 at 1637 bytes and the ladder's first and last cells.
69.final_note: F68's fraglist cap is reachable once every datagram has the same length; the 20-byte price anomaly is arithmetic (127*1280/64 against 126*1280/64), not a price.

70.title: the branch, and its boundary
70.claim: `skb_condense()`'s early return is taken on the head's tailroom, not on a constant: an aggregate head arrives linear and already carries the whole aggregate's truesize, `data_len == 0` skips the block entirely, and the strictly-greater comparison with `rcvbuf >> 1` decides whether the queue's bill collapses.
70.repro: instrument `differ592`, mode `cond`; 9 arms × 2 attempts × 2 boots, a kprobe on `skb_condense()` at DWARF-derived offsets (len 112, data_len 116, tail 188, end 192, truesize 216, flags 126) plus five counters; a filler at 250 ms puts `rmem` exactly on `rcvbuf >> 1`.
70.expected: `skb_condense()` is called only when `rmem > rcvbuf >> 1`; the early return compares `data_len > end - tail`; the last line sets `skb->truesize = SKB_TRUESIZE(skb_end_offset(skb))`.
70.actual: Six datagrams of 512 through the fraglist door: head `len=512 dlen=0 tail=556 end=704 ts=7680 fl=0`, segments 2-6 at 1280; `__pskb_pull_tail` 0 calls in all 36 attempts. `SO_RCVBUF(19200)` puts `rmem` exactly on 19200 (`c_eq`): the burst leaves 14080 with 5 calls; one more filler (20480) gives 7680 with 6 calls. Five datagrams of 512 and one of 200: the head arrives at 7360 and the queue gains 7360. The linear door also totals 7680 but each record is 1280.
70.limits: All three early-return clauses are unreachable in this instrument except the first; clause 3 needs SKBFL_PURE_ZEROCOPY (F72), clause 2 needs a second consumer (F72).
70.regression: `skb_condense()` is called iff `rmem > rcvbuf >> 1`, and the queue's bill collapses only above half a buffer; a test pins the 14080/7680 pair on either side of the boundary.

71.title: the skb behind `skb_condense()`'s first clause, measured at the function
71.claim: The first clause of `skb_condense()` is measured at the function: an aggregate delivered whole to a `UDP_GRO` socket reaches the queue with `data_len` 2560 against 148 bytes of tailroom, so the early return is taken by the first clause alone, one enqueue and one call against six and six on a plain socket.
71.repro: instrument `differ593`, mode `gro`; 18 arms × 2 attempts × 2 boots, receiver with two sockets (5000 plain, 5001 `UDP_GRO`), seven kprobes including the enqueue door; three head sizes for the byte boundary.
71.expected: `skb_condense()` returns early when `data_len > end - tail`; `udp_unexpected_gso()` refuses `SKB_GSO_FRAGLIST` without `ACCEPT_FRAGLIST`, and `UDP_GRO` sets only `ACCEPT_L4`; `ACCEPT_FRAGLIST` is set by `udp_allow_gso()` (vxlan, geneve, bareudp).
71.actual: Six datagrams of 512 through `rx-udp-gro-forwarding` to the `UDP_GRO` socket: `f593enq len=3072 dlen=2560 tail=556 end=704 ts=7680 fl=0` and one `f593cond` call -- 2560 > 148, clause 1 alone, `__pskb_pull_tail` not called, queue keeps 7680, application gets one 3072-byte datagram. Boundaries 148/140/484 pinned to the byte; above half the same two datagrams cost 1280 against 2240 below; a tap sets `cloned` and blocks the pull (2240, 0 pulls); fraglist on `UDP_GRO` equals fraglist on a plain socket (6 enqueues, 7680).
71.limits: `SKBFL_PURE_ZEROCOPY` absent (clause 3 unmeasurable here); the page-frag branch of `skb_gro_receive()` never taken (`head_frag` 0); a real NIC not measured.
71.regression: `data_len == end - tail` pulls and one more byte returns; a test pins the three boundaries and the one-enqueue/two-enqueue contrast.

72.title: what a user page does to the two UDP GRO doors, measured at the doors
72.claim: `skb_gro_receive()` refuses a zerocopy datagram outright, so a zerocopy burst reaches the forwarding hook as six packets through the linear door while the fraglist door merges the same six into one; each enqueue record is charged `end + 576 + PAGE_ALIGN(payload + page offset)` for a zerocopy skb and `end + 576` otherwise, so the sender's buffer alignment sets the price.
72.repro: instrument `differ594`, modes `cl`, `zc`; 13 arms × 2 attempts × 2 boots; sender with SO_ZEROCOPY/MSG_ZEROCOPY, receiver with an optional packet socket and filter, forward chain with a `log` rule so the rule's own packet count is a number.
72.expected: `skb_gro_receive()` has `if (skb_zcopy(p) || skb_zcopy(skb)) return -ETOOMANYREFS;`; `skb_gro_receive_list()` has no such check; the enqueue price is `end + 576` plus, for zerocopy, `PAGE_ALIGN(payload + page offset)` (F73).
72.actual: Zerocopy six 512-byte datagrams reach the hook as six packets with `uh->len` 520 each (linear), and as one packet of 3080 (fraglist). One 512-byte zerocopy datagram costs 5056 at page offset 0 and 9152 at offset 3600; 5000 bytes cost 9152 at offset 0; a copied 512-byte datagram costs 1280. Copy counts: six on the linear door, one on the fraglist aggregate. At `SO_RCVBUF` 19200 (R 38400) a 64-datagram zerocopy burst from offset 0 leaves 7 with 57 drops; from offset 3600 it leaves 4.
72.limits: IPv6, TCP, tunnels, CHECKSUM_COMPLETE and a real NIC were not measured; the `skb_cloned` bit is set by a tap and blocks the pull.
72.regression: Zerocopy is refused by the linear GRO door and merged by the fraglist door; a test pins six-vs-one packet and the per-offset charge.

73.title: where the page charge comes from, and who clones on the receive path
73.claim: The page charge is made in `zerocopy_fill_skb_from_iter()` as `skb->truesize += PAGE_ALIGN(copied + start)`, where `start` is the iov's page offset, so one 512-byte datagram costs 5056 at offset 0 and 9152 at offset 3600; `skb_clone()` on this path is `skb_segment()`'s, once per `frag_list` member, and `MSG_SPLICE_PAGES` is cleared by `__sys_sendto()` before it reaches the kernel.
73.repro: instrument `differ595`, modes `all`, `chg`, `cln`, `spl`; 18 arms × 2 attempts × 2 boots plus one diagnostic boot; the sender changes only the place of the payload in its page; a probe at `skb_clone()` prints the return address (`caller=$stack0:x64`, `nokaslr`).
73.expected: `net/core/datagram.c:662` does `skb->truesize += PAGE_ALIGN(copied + start)`; `net/core/skbuff.c:4933` is `nskb = skb_clone(list_skb, GFP_ATOMIC)` inside `skb_segment()`; `net/socket.c:2277` does `flags &= ~MSG_INTERNAL_SENDMSG_FLAGS`, the mask including `MSG_SPLICE_PAGES`.
73.actual: 512 bytes at offset 0: 5056 = 960 + 4096; at offset 3600: 9152 = 960 + 8192; 1200 at 3600: 9152; 4097 at 0: 9152; 5000 at 0: 9152; 5000 at 3600: 13248. The same number is read at `__dev_queue_xmit`, `skb_copy_ubufs`, `ip_forward`, `ip_local_deliver`, `udp_rcv` and `/proc/net/udp`. Five `skb_clone()` calls from one return address `0xffffffff829134c4`, inside `skb_segment()`; `skb_segment_list()` clones none (7680 on the head). `MSG_SPLICE_PAGES`: `__ip_append_data` sees `flags = 0`, `skb_splice_from_iter` 0 calls, the datagram costs 1280 (512 bytes) and 8448 (5000).
73.limits: Only veth and this tree; `splice(pipe -> socket)` was not measured.
73.regression: Zerocopy charge equals `960 + PAGE_ALIGN(payload + page offset)`; a test pins 5056/9152/13248 for the three placements.
73.final_note: F72's charge is not one page per payload: it is PAGE_ALIGN(payload + page offset), measured at three placements.

74.title: what the offset charge does to the queue, and where the head of a copied datagram comes from
74.claim: The receive queue holds `floor(sk_rcvbuf / charge)` datagrams and the boundary is one byte of the socket's own request (`SO_RCVBUF` 17695 keeps 6, 17696 keeps 7); the same 64 datagrams are 7 or 4 depending on the sender's page offset, which the socket cannot see, and a 200-byte zerocopy datagram can have the offset charge erased by `skb_condense()` above half a buffer.
74.repro: instrument `differ596`, modes `q` (21 arms) and `h` (9 arms); 30 arms × 2 attempts × 2 boots, one process per mode; `SO_RCVBUF` sweep, mixed charge sequences, 200-byte arms, and a sweep of head sizes for the allocation class.
74.expected: `__udp_enqueue_schedule_skb()` refuses when `rmem + size > rcvbuf`, strictly; `skb_condense()` collapses the head's truesize above half a buffer; `kmalloc_reserve()` uses `SKB_SMALL_HEAD_CACHE_SIZE` as the small-head ceiling.
74.actual: R 38400/51200/76800/102400 with charge 5056 keep 7/10/15/20 (rmem 35392/50560/75840/101120) and with 9152 keep 4/5/8/11 (36608/45760/73216/100672); `SO_RCVBUF` 17695 (R 35390) keeps 6, 17696 (R 35392 = 7*5056) keeps 7; two arms leave rmem equal to rcvbuf and keep all 64 (323584, 585728). Mixed at R 51200: 7 kept with rmem 47680 although floor(51200/9152) = 5; 64 datagrams of 200 bytes keep 18 with 33664 = 4*5056 + 14*960; the head-size step is at payload 325/326 (end 384 → 704, ts 960 → 1280), the small-head object size read from the boot's own slab cache is 704.
74.limits: Charges of mixed arms beyond the 16th record are derived from the stride; `SO_RCVBUFFORCE`, IPv6, TCP, tunnels and a real NIC were not measured.
74.regression: The queue's capacity is `floor(R/charge)` and the charge is set by the sender's page offset; a test pins 17695/17696 and the 7-vs-4 pair.
